snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew 'Elohim' is plural—Gods—but paired with a singular verb 'created' (bara). This grammatical peculiarity has puzzled Jewish scholars for millennia. The Restoration resolves it: the Godhead acts in perfect unity, and Abraham later shows us the plural is literal—multiple divine Beings organized the earth under the Father's direction.
snippets.label: Hebrew

snippets.snippet_text: Moses clarifies what Genesis omits: 'For I, the Lord God, created all things... spiritually, before they were naturally upon the face of the earth.' Everything existed in spirit form first. This dual creation—spiritual then physical—maps perfectly onto the doctrine of pre-mortal existence and the necessity of mortality for progression.
snippets.label: Restoration

snippets.snippet_text: Abraham witnesses the Grand Council before the Creation: 'The Lord said... We will go down... and we will prove them herewith.' The Creation accounts are the execution of this pre-mortal council decision. The same intelligences present there—including us—are now experiencing the probation that council planned.
snippets.label: Cross-Ref

snippets.snippet_text: Ancient Near Eastern texts often depict gods creating humans to serve as slaves. Genesis radically inverts this: Adam becomes 'a living soul' (nephesh chayyah), the same phrase used for animals in Genesis 1:21—but humanity receives the divine image and dominion. We are not divine servants but divine children.
snippets.label: Historical

snippets.snippet_text: Eve coming from Adam's side while he sleeps, then becoming his wife, carries profound temple symbolism. President Spencer W. Kimball taught that Adam's sleep was 'a deep sleep' like a trance or vision, and that Eve's creation was likely more sublime than the rib account suggests. The endowment ceremony presents this event as sacred instruction, not biology lesson.
snippets.label: Restoration

snippets.snippet_text: Joseph Smith taught, 'The head God called together the Gods and sat in grand council to bring forth the world' (King Follett Discourse). Abraham chapter 4 is the closest scriptural account of that council. This isn't Mormon folklore—it's canonized scripture revealing the plural divine council pattern found throughout the Old Testament.
snippets.label: Prophetic
